h1: A warm desk in a 60°F house
kicker_tail: one cold office in Hamden, CT
sub: A 10 by 12 office that faces north and has two doorways with no doors in them. These are the things that could keep the typing going with the oil heat turned down to 60°F, each one priced against the space heater already in the room.
meta_description: Heated desk and floor mats, under-desk radiant panels, wool arm warmers, and felt panels for a cold home office, each priced per hour against a 1,125 W heater.
legend: Everything here was in stock with a posted price when we checked it. Powered items show rated watts and what an hour costs at 28¢ per kWh; where a seller doesn't publish watts, the number is our estimate and is marked that way. Arm warmers had to have a thumbhole and leave the fingers bare. Any heater meant to sit near felt had to be rated zero-clearance, and the things we checked and rejected are listed at the bottom with the reason. Prices as of October 11, 2026; listings change.
vornado_box: The Vornado VH200 on medium draws 1,125 W. At United Illuminating's 28¢ per kWh that is 31.5¢ an hour, or about $53 a month of eight-hour workdays. Every powered item on this page shows its cost as a share of that number, and only one of them, the WhisperHeat, costs more than a quarter of it.
hands_box: The muscles that bend your fingers sit in your forearm. Researchers at the US Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine warmed people's forearms while leaving their hands bare, and finger skin rose from about 50°F to 55°F, which went with roughly 50% better dexterity. Another study found that warm hands lose their dexterity anyway when the forearm muscles are cold, which is why the arm warmers come first here and why a longer sleeve beats a wrist-length one.
correction_box: An earlier chat guessed that heated desk mats draw 20 to 25 W, but the plug-in pads that publish a number say 85 to 100 W, and Giambwa lists 95 W. That is still only about 8% of the Vornado, and because the thermostats cycle on and off, the real draw runs lower.
safety_box: Never put the Vornado or any coil or fan heater inside the felt. The only heaters that belong in there are rated zero-clearance, like Cozy Legs. Wool felt chars and won't catch until around 570 to 600°C, while polyester felt melts near 250°C; both are far above a 130°F panel, but wool is the better neighbor. Never cover a heated mat with felt, a blanket, or anything else.
tally_hint: Add powered items to the cocoon and the tally sums their watts and hourly cost against the Vornado's 31.5¢; a Giambwa mat, a Cozy Legs panel, and a heated vest come to 257 W, about 7¢ an hour.

desk.title: Heated desk mats
desk.intro: A desk mat is the only heater here that touches your hands, which is the whole complaint. The three below top out between 122°F and 131°F, and low-temperature burns can happen with all-day skin contact somewhere between 111°F and 124°F, so let the mat warm the keyboard area and keep your wrists off it when it's on high.

arms.title: Wool arm warmers
arms.intro: These cost nothing to run and they warm the forearm, where the finger muscles are. Every pair has a thumbhole and leaves the fingers free for typing. Most wool thumbhole warmers sold in the US stop at the wrist, 7 to 10 inches long, so the 45 cm pairs that reach toward the elbow are here whenever we could find one.

floor.title: Heated floor mats
floor.intro: Drew stands for part of the day, and most heated floor mats aren't meant to be stood on. Cozy Products' rubber FW and FWB are the exceptions, and only on hard floors; the warning rules out carpet, hardwood, and linoleum because the rubber may discolor them. The 55 W carbon-crystal mats cost the least to run but are for sitting, and no mat on this page should ever be covered.

panel.title: Under-desk radiant panels
panel.intro: The spec to look for is zero-clearance, meaning the panel can touch combustible material; Cozy Legs is ETL-certified for it, and the University of Washington's fire-safety rules name it as allowed under desks. Stuck flat under the desktop it goes up and down with a sit/stand desk, while the floor-standing panels only help when you sit. A panel and a floor mat both aim at the legs, so inside a felt cave one of the two may be enough, and the tally shows what dropping one saves.

felt.title: Felt panels for a kotatsu cave
felt.intro: Clamp-on panels rise with the desktop, so the cave only exists while you sit, which is also when legs get cold. The side you sit on can't be a panel, and without a lap blanket closing it most of the trapped heat leaks out there. Thicker felt holds more: VIVO's panels are 1 inch, about eight times Vari's felt at ⅛ inch.

bonus.title: Help for the hands from elsewhere
bonus.intro: A heated vest draws about 12 W on high, and a full battery costs about 1¢ to recharge. When the core is warm the body clamps down less on blood flow to the hands, so a vest works on your fingers from about two feet away. The other two items here work on the hands directly and cost almost nothing to run.

cut.title: Checked and left out
cut.intro: We looked at these and passed, and each one has its reason next to it. A few of those reasons, like the 3-foot clearance rule on commercial desk heaters, ended up shaping the rest of the page.

notes.giambwa: The only desk mat here that publishes its wattage, which is where the 95 W in the correction comes from. On its top setting it costs about 2.7¢ an hour, roughly a twelfth of the Vornado, and it is the cheapest of the three to buy.
notes.tulpock: Its hottest setting is the coolest of the three, which makes it the better pick if your wrists will rest on it for hours. It also has the most reviews of any desk mat we found.
notes.icasso: Big enough to put the keyboard and the mouse both on heat. The 131°F setting is warmer than skin should sit against all day, so use high to warm up and then turn it down.
notes.laindesign: It pairs the long 45 cm length with sizing for a man's hand, for less than half what the alpaca pair costs. Shipping from Latvia brings the long pair to $45.
notes.zauberhand: Cut for men, with the duties already paid, so the price you see is the price. It stops a little past the wrist, so it does less for the forearm muscles than the long pairs.
notes.dilling: The easiest pair here to send back if typing in arm warmers doesn't take. The thin knit should sit under a shirt cuff without bunching.
notes.marakash: One of the few 45 cm pairs we found, long enough to cover most of the forearm. The photos show it on women, so check the hand opening against your own before ordering.
notes.woolly: If the Army study holds, this is the most warmth per arm on the page, and it has the highest price of the arm warmers to match. The undyed alpaca reaches all the way to the elbow.
notes.cozy-fw: Its maker sells it for standing workstations, which is why it leads despite a 4.0★ rating. It costs about 3.4¢ an hour, around a tenth of the Vornado.
notes.cozy-fwb: The same rubber mat made 13 inches longer, for $13 more and 15 more watts. The extra length lets you stand with your feet apart and both of them still on heat.
notes.livtribe: At 55 W it is the cheapest heat on the floor, about 1.5¢ an hour. Use it while seated and slide it aside when the desk goes up.
notes.hodeamy: Nearly the same mat as the Livtribe, squarer and a dollar cheaper. Pick whichever shape fits the space under the desk.
notes.toasty: One device that can warm your feet or, folded upright, your shins. With no auto-off, it needs a switched power strip or a reliable habit.
notes.cozylegs: The panel the rest of the plan is built around, since it can sit inside felt and is thin enough to stick flat under the desktop. It costs about 4.2¢ an hour at 150 W, or 2.1¢ on the optional low switch.
notes.deskheat: A thin film that heats about twice the area of Cozy Legs at 100 W. We couldn't confirm a zero-clearance rating, so it stays out of the felt plan.
notes.cl2: The cheaper Cozy Legs carries the same zero-clearance rating, but on the feet it ships with, it only warms you while you sit. At 200 W it also draws more than the Classic.
notes.whisper: The most heat for the legs on this page, and at about 9¢ an hour the closest thing here to running the Vornado. It wraps your legs while you sit and does nothing once you stand.
notes.vivo-kit: Three panels make a box with one open side, which is the side you sit on. At $310 for the set it is the most expensive way to find out whether the cave works.
notes.sturion-kit: The same front-and-two-sides layout as the VIVO kit for about a third of the price.
notes.ergo: Only a front panel, so it blocks the draft across your shins and leaves the sides open. What it adds is a tray for the cords that a mat and a panel bring with them.
notes.spruce: A quarter inch of real wool, from an aircraft-parts supplier, which is where we found the cheapest all-wool felt thick enough to matter. Expect to cut it yourself and clip it on.
notes.filzfelt: The wool felt you would choose for looks, and at $185 a yard it costs like it. At 3 mm it is about half as thick as the Aircraft Spruce felt, so you trade some warmth for color.
notes.vivo-skirt: For $50 you can find out whether closing in the desk does anything before you buy panels. A permies.com thread on kotatsu skirts reports a sheet draped over a desk warming a whole 10×12 room by a few degrees.
notes.venustas: The one you could wear at a desk all day without looking dressed for a ski lift. On high it draws about an eighth of what a desk mat does.
notes.ororo: Costs $40 more than the Venustas and looks more like outerwear. Pick it if you'd also wear it outside.
notes.valleyx: A heated pouch the mouse hand slides into, drawing about 5 W. It does nothing for the keyboard hand, so it backs up the arm warmers instead of replacing them.
notes.glorious: At the same temperature, hardwood feels warm under your wrists where aluminum or plastic feels cold, because it pulls heat away more slowly. At $20 it is the cheapest unpowered thing here that touches your hands.

footer: No affiliate links, and nobody paid for a spot. This is a shopping list and not safety advice, so follow each maker's instructions. Measure your desktop's thickness before buying clamp-on panels; VIVO's clamps fit 0.4 to 1.4 inches. Prices checked October 11, 2026.
